description: Intermediate/advanced Spanish sentence cards: subjunctive, tenses, se, ser/estar, por/para, connectors, false friends, idioms and proverbs. Each back gives the translation and the key grammar point; Latin/Arabic/Germanic etymology (with Dutch and English cognates) sits in the extra field as a memory hook.

notes.front: Espero que todo salga bien.
notes.back:
I hope it all turns out well.
• esperar que + present subjunctive (salga).
notes.extra: Etymology: salir < Lat. salire 'to leap' — cf. Eng. salient, somersault. Leap → go out.

notes.front: No creo que sea una buena idea.
notes.back:
I don't think it's a good idea.
• Negated belief (no creer que) forces subjunctive sea; creo que es would be indicative.
notes.extra: Etymology: creer < Lat. credere — Eng. credit, creed, Du. krediet.

notes.front: Cuando llegues, avísame.
notes.back:
Let me know when you arrive.
• cuando + subjunctive for future events (habitual = indicative).
notes.extra: Etymology: llegar < Lat. plicare 'to fold (the sails)' → arrive — cf. Eng. apply, ply. avisar < ad visum — Eng. advise, Du. advies.

notes.front: Es importante que sepas la verdad.
notes.back:
It's important that you know the truth.
• Impersonal judgment (es importante que) + subjunctive sepas.
notes.extra: Etymology: saber < Lat. sapere 'to taste, be wise' — Eng. sapient, savour, Fr. savoir. Knowing = tasting.

notes.front: Quiero que me lo digas ahora mismo.
notes.back:
I want you to tell me right now.
• querer que + subjunctive when subjects differ (quiero decir = same subject, infinitive).
notes.extra: Etymology: querer < Lat. quaerere 'to seek' — Eng. question, query, inquire. Seeking → wanting → loving.

notes.front: Dudo que venga a la fiesta.
notes.back:
I doubt he'll come to the party.
• Doubt triggers subjunctive venga.
notes.extra: Etymology: dudar < Lat. dubitare — Eng. doubt, dubious, Du. dubieus, and likely Du. dubben 'to waver'.

notes.front: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
notes.back:
I'm glad you're here.
• Emotion + que → subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: alegre < Lat. alacer 'lively' — Eng. alacrity, It. allegro (the music tempo you know from Du./Eng. usage).

notes.front: Ojalá llueva mañana.
notes.back:
I hope it rains tomorrow.
• ojalá + subjunctive, always.
notes.extra: Etymology: ojalá < Arabic wa-šā' allāh 'and may God will it' — same phrase as inshallah. llover < Lat. pluere — Eng. pluvial, Fr. pluie.

notes.front: Que tengas un buen viaje.
notes.back:
Have a good trip.
• Bare que + subjunctive = wish formula (short for espero que).
notes.extra: Etymology: viaje < Lat. viaticum 'provisions for the road' (< via) — Eng. voyage, viaduct, Du. viaduct.

notes.front: No hay nadie que lo entienda.
notes.back:
There's nobody who understands it.
• Non-existent antecedent (nadie) → subjunctive entienda.
notes.extra: Etymology: entender < Lat. intendere 'to stretch toward' — Eng. intend, intense, Du. intens. Understanding = stretching the mind toward.

notes.front: Busco a alguien que hable alemán.
notes.back:
I'm looking for someone who speaks German.
• Hypothetical person → subjunctive; que habla = a specific known person.
notes.extra: Etymology: hablar < Lat. fabulari 'to tell stories' — Eng. fable, fabulous, Du. fabel. Speaking = storytelling.

notes.front: Es posible que tarde un poco.
notes.back:
It may take a while / he may be a bit late.
• Possibility → subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: tardar < Lat. tardare — Eng. tardy, retard, Fr. tard.

notes.front: Aunque cueste mucho, lo compraré.
notes.back:
Even if it costs a lot, I'll buy it.
• aunque + subjunctive = 'even if' (unknown); + indicative = 'even though' (fact).
notes.extra: Etymology: costar < Lat. constare 'to stand at (a price)' — Eng. cost, constant, Du. kosten (same Latin source).

notes.front: Te llamo para que no te preocupes.
notes.back:
I'm calling so you won't worry.
• para que + subjunctive (purpose, different subjects).
notes.extra: Etymology: preocupar < Lat. praeoccupare 'to seize beforehand' — Eng. preoccupied. Worry = your mind seized in advance.

notes.front: No es que no quiera, es que no puedo.
notes.back:
It's not that I don't want to, it's that I can't.
• no es que + subjunctive; es que + indicative. Very common spoken pattern.
notes.extra: Etymology: poder < Vulgar Lat. *potere — Eng. potent, possible, Du. potentie.

notes.front: Más vale que te des prisa.
notes.back:
You'd better hurry up.
• más vale que + subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: valer < Lat. valere 'to be strong, be worth' — Eng. value, valid, prevail, Du. valide. Roman letters closed with vale 'farewell' (= be strong); Spanish ¡vale! 'OK' is the same verb.

notes.front: Puede que tengas razón.
notes.back:
You may be right.
• puede que + subjunctive. Synonym of quizás.
notes.extra: Etymology: razón < Lat. ratio — Eng. reason, ratio, Du. ratio, rationeel. Tener razón = 'to have reason', like Fr. avoir raison.

notes.front: Prefiero que nos veamos mañana.
notes.back:
I'd rather we meet tomorrow.
• Preference + different subject → subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: ver < Lat. videre — Eng. video, evident, provide, Du. video, evident.

notes.front: Temo que sea demasiado tarde.
notes.back:
I'm afraid it's too late.
• Fear → subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: temer < Lat. timere — Eng. timid, intimidate.

notes.front: En cuanto sepa algo, te aviso.
notes.back:
As soon as I hear anything, I'll let you know.
• en cuanto + subjunctive for future reference; note colloquial present te aviso instead of future.
notes.extra: Etymology: cuanto < Lat. quantus — Eng. quantity, quantum, Du. kwantiteit.

notes.front: Si tuviera más tiempo, viajaría más.
notes.back:
If I had more time, I'd travel more.
• Second conditional: imperfect subjunctive (tuviera) + conditional (viajaría).
notes.extra: Etymology: tener < Lat. tenere 'to hold' — Eng. tenant, contain, tenacious. Holding → having.

notes.front: Me pidió que le ayudara con la mudanza.
notes.back:
He asked me to help him with the move.
• Reported request: past main verb → imperfect subjunctive ayudara.
notes.extra: Etymology: ayudar < Lat. adiutare — Eng. aid, adjutant, Du. adjudant (the helper-officer).

notes.front: Si fuera tú, no lo haría.
notes.back:
If I were you, I wouldn't do it.
• Hypothetical si + imperfect subjunctive; English keeps the same relic ('if I were').
notes.extra: Etymology: hacer < Lat. facere — Eng. fact, factory, manufacture, Du. feit (< Fr. fait < factum).

notes.front: Ojalá pudiera quedarme más tiempo.
notes.back:
I wish I could stay longer.
• ojalá + imperfect subjunctive = unreal present wish.
notes.extra: Etymology: quedar < Lat. quietare 'to quiet' → stay — Eng. quiet, quit, Du. kwijt (all from quietus: settled → released → rid of).

notes.front: Hablas como si lo supieras todo.
notes.back:
You talk as if you knew everything.
• como si always takes imperfect/pluperfect subjunctive — like Latin quasi + subjunctive.

notes.front: Quisiera reservar una mesa para dos.
notes.back:
I'd like to book a table for two.
• quisiera = extra-polite querría; frozen imperfect subjunctive used as courtesy form.
notes.extra: Etymology: mesa < Lat. mensa (the school word for 'table' — Du. students know mensa as canteen).

notes.front: Si no fuera por ti, no lo habría logrado.
notes.back:
If it weren't for you, I wouldn't have managed it.
• Mixed conditional: present-unreal si-clause + past-result conditional perfect.
notes.extra: Etymology: lograr < Lat. lucrari 'to gain' — Eng. lucrative, Du. lucratief.

notes.front: Me gustaría que vinieras conmigo.
notes.back:
I'd like you to come with me.
• Conditional in main clause pulls the subordinate into imperfect subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: venir < Lat. venire — Eng. convene, advent, Du. avontuur (< Old Fr. aventure < advenire 'what comes at you').

notes.front: Sería mejor que lo dejaras para mañana.
notes.back:
It would be better if you left it for tomorrow.
• sería mejor que + imperfect subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: dejar < Lat. laxare 'to loosen' — Eng. lax, relax, Du. laks. Loosening your grip → leaving something.

notes.front: Aunque me lo pidieras de rodillas, diría que no.
notes.back:
Even if you begged me on your knees, I'd say no.
• Hypothetical concession: aunque + imperfect subjunctive + conditional.
notes.extra: Etymology: rodilla < Lat. rotella, diminutive of rota 'wheel' (the round kneecap) — Eng. rotate, Du. rotonde.

notes.front: Si lo hubiera sabido, no habría venido.
notes.back:
If I had known, I wouldn't have come.
• Third conditional: pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera sabido) + conditional perfect (habría venido). Spoken Spanish often uses hubiera in both halves.

notes.front: Me habría encantado acompañarte.
notes.back:
I would have loved to come with you.
• Conditional perfect for unrealized past.
notes.extra: Etymology: encantar < Lat. incantare 'to sing a spell over' — Eng. enchant, chant, incantation. Liking something = being bewitched.

notes.front: ¿Qué harías si te tocara la lotería?
notes.back:
What would you do if you won the lottery?
• tocar (lit. 'to touch') = to fall to someone by luck: me toca = it's my turn / I won.
notes.extra: Etymology: lotería < Du./Low Germanic lot 'lot, share' via Fr. — the Dutch word lot (loterij!) travelled into Romance, not the other way.

notes.front: Actuó como si nada hubiera pasado.
notes.back:
He acted as if nothing had happened.
• como si + pluperfect subjunctive for a past pretence.
notes.extra: Etymology: pasar < Vulgar Lat. passare < passus 'step' — Eng. pass, pace, Du. passeren, pas.

notes.front: Fue una lástima que no pudieras venir.
notes.back:
It was a pity you couldn't come.
• Past evaluation → imperfect subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: lástima < lastimar < Vulgar Lat. blastemare < Gk blasphemein — Eng. blasphemy AND blame are the same word split in two. A pity = a wound by words.

notes.front: Mientras cenábamos, se fue la luz.
notes.back:
While we were having dinner, the power went out.
• Imperfect = background scene; preterite = the interrupting event. The core past-tense contrast.
notes.extra: Etymology: cenar < Lat. cenare; cena was the main Roman meal. luz < lux — Eng. lucid, Lucifer ('light-bearer').

notes.front: Cuando era niño, veraneábamos en la costa.
notes.back:
When I was a kid, we spent summers on the coast.
• Imperfect for habitual past ('used to').
notes.extra: Etymology: veranear < verano < Lat. veranum (tempus) 'spring-time' — Eng. vernal. Spanish shifted spring → summer.

notes.front: Ayer conocí a tus padres.
notes.back:
Yesterday I met your parents.
• conocer in preterite = 'met (for the first time)'; imperfect conocía = 'knew'.
notes.extra: Etymology: conocer < Lat. cognoscere — Eng. recognize, cognition. Deeper: Lat. gno-, Eng. know and Du. kennen are all the same Proto-Indo-European (PIE) root *ǵneh₃-.

notes.front: No quiso ayudarme.
notes.back:
He refused to help me.
• querer in preterite = 'refused' (negative) / 'tried to' (positive); imperfect no quería = merely 'didn't want to'.

notes.front: Supe la noticia esta mañana.
notes.back:
I found out the news this morning.
• saber in preterite = 'found out'; imperfect sabía = 'knew'.
notes.extra: Etymology: noticia < Lat. notitia 'acquaintance' < notus 'known' — Eng. notice, notion, Du. notitie.

notes.front: Podía oír el mar desde la habitación.
notes.back:
I could hear the sea from the room.
• Imperfect podía = ongoing ability; preterite pude = managed to (one occasion).
notes.extra: Etymology: oír < Lat. audire — Eng. audio, audience, obey (< oboedire 'listen toward'), Du. audio.

notes.front: De repente, alguien llamó a la puerta.
notes.back:
Suddenly, someone knocked on the door.
• Preterite for the sudden event.
notes.extra: Etymology: de repente < Lat. repente 'suddenly'. llamar < Lat. clamare 'to shout' — Eng. claim, exclaim, clamor, Du. reclame (advertising = repeated shouting, re-clamare).

notes.front: Antes fumaba, pero lo dejé hace años.
notes.back:
I used to smoke, but I quit years ago.
• Imperfect for the old habit, preterite for the clean break; hace + time = 'ago'.
notes.extra: Etymology: fumar < Lat. fumare — Eng. fume, perfume ('through smoke'), Du. parfum.

notes.front: Estaba a punto de salir cuando sonó el teléfono.
notes.back:
I was about to leave when the phone rang.
• estar a punto de + infinitive = to be about to.
notes.extra: Etymology: sonar < Lat. sonare — Eng. sound, resonate, sonata, Du. resoneren.

notes.front: Tenía tanta hambre que me comí dos platos.
notes.back:
I was so hungry I ate two plates.
• comerse (reflexive) = eat up completely, emphatic.
notes.extra: Etymology: plato < Vulgar Lat. *plattus < Gk platys 'flat' — Eng. plate, plateau, Du. plat ('flat' — same word, Dutch kept the original meaning).

notes.front: Nos conocimos hace diez años.
notes.back:
We met ten years ago.
• Reciprocal nos + preterite; hace + time span = 'ago' (lit. 'it makes ten years' — cf. Fr. il y a).

notes.front: Iba a llamarte, pero se me olvidó.
notes.back:
I was going to call you, but I forgot.
• ir a in imperfect = unfulfilled plan; se me olvidó = 'no-fault' construction (the forgetting happened to me).
notes.extra: Etymology: olvidar < Vulgar Lat. *oblitare < oblivisci — Eng. oblivion, oblivious.

notes.front: Serán las diez, más o menos.
notes.back:
It must be about ten o'clock.
• Future tense used for present conjecture — a use Dutch/English lack (Du. 'het zal een uur of tien zijn' comes close!).

notes.front: Estará en una reunión, por eso no contesta.
notes.back:
She's probably in a meeting, that's why she isn't answering.
• Future of conjecture again.
notes.extra: Etymology: contestar < Lat. contestari 'to call to witness' — false friend of Eng. contest; in Spanish it just means 'to answer'.

notes.front: ¿Quién llamará a estas horas?
notes.back:
Who could be calling at this hour?
• Future tense = wondering aloud about the present.
notes.extra: Etymology: hora < Lat./Gk hora — Eng. hour, Du. uur: all three are the same borrowed word.

notes.front: Tendría unos cuarenta años cuando lo conocí.
notes.back:
He must have been about forty when I met him.
• Conditional = conjecture about the past (mirror of the future-of-probability).
notes.extra: Etymology: cuarenta < Lat. quadraginta — Eng. quarantine: originally forty days of ship isolation (Venetian quarantena).

notes.front: Ya habrán llegado a casa.
notes.back:
They must have arrived home by now.
• Future perfect for conjecture about a completed action.

notes.front: Dijo que vendría, pero no apareció.
notes.back:
He said he would come, but he never showed up.
• Conditional as 'future in the past' (reported speech), exactly like Eng. would / Du. zou.
notes.extra: Etymology: aparecer < Lat. apparescere — Eng. appear, apparition, Du. apparitie.

notes.front: ¿Dónde estarán mis llaves?
notes.back:
Where on earth are my keys?
• Future of probability with a self-directed question.
notes.extra: Etymology: llave < Lat. clavis — Eng. clavicle ('little key' bone; Du. sleutelbeen is a literal calque of that!), clef, enclave.

notes.front: Todavía no he terminado el informe.
notes.back:
I still haven't finished the report.
• Present perfect with todavía no; peninsular Spanish uses this tense far more than Latin America.
notes.extra: Etymology: terminar < Lat. terminare < terminus 'boundary stone' — Eng. terminate, term, Du. termijn.

notes.front: ¿Alguna vez has estado en México?
notes.back:
Have you ever been to Mexico?
• alguna vez = 'ever' with the experiential perfect.
notes.extra: Etymology: vez < Lat. vicis 'turn, change' — Eng. vice versa, vicissitude.

notes.front: Cuando llegué, ya se habían ido.
notes.back:
When I arrived, they had already left.
• Pluperfect (habían ido) for the earlier of two past events — works just like Du. waren al vertrokken.

notes.front: He estado pensando en lo que dijiste.
notes.back:
I've been thinking about what you said.
• Perfect progressive: haber + estado + gerund.
notes.extra: Etymology: pensar < Lat. pensare 'to weigh' — Eng. pensive, compensate, Du. pensioen (a payment 'weighed out'). Thinking = weighing.

notes.front: Nunca había visto nada igual.
notes.back:
I had never seen anything like it.
• Pluperfect + double negative (nunca... nada), standard in Spanish.
notes.extra: Etymology: igual < Lat. aequalis — Eng. equal, Du. egaal (via Fr. égal).

notes.front: Últimamente he tenido mucho trabajo.
notes.back:
Lately I've had a lot of work.
• últimamente pairs naturally with the present perfect.
notes.extra: Etymology: último < Lat. ultimus — Eng. ultimate, Du. ultimatum. trabajo < Vulgar Lat. tripaliare 'to torture on the tripalium' (three-stake device) — same grim root as Fr. travail and Eng. travel.

notes.front: Ya hemos hablado de esto mil veces.
notes.back: We've already talked about this a thousand times.
notes.extra: Hook: mil veces = hyperbolic 'a thousand times', same idiom as Du. duizend keer.

notes.front: Para cuando te des cuenta, ya habré acabado.
notes.back:
By the time you notice, I'll already be done.
• Future perfect (habré acabado) + para cuando + subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: acabar < a + cabo < Lat. caput 'head, end' — Eng. cape, capital, Du. kaap. To finish = to bring to a head.

notes.front: Me estás tomando el pelo, ¿no?
notes.back:
You're pulling my leg, right?
• tomar el pelo = to tease (lit. 'take the hair').
notes.extra:
Etymology: pelo < Lat. pilus — Eng. depilate, caterpillar (Old Fr. chatepelose 'hairy cat').
Hook: Du. iemand in de maling nemen.

notes.front: Ese coche cuesta un ojo de la cara.
notes.back: That car costs an arm and a leg (lit. 'an eye from the face').
notes.extra: Etymology: ojo < Lat. oculus — Eng. ocular, binoculars, Du. oculair, monocle.

notes.front: Mi abuela no tiene pelos en la lengua.
notes.back: My grandma doesn't mince words (lit. 'has no hairs on her tongue').
notes.extra: Etymology: lengua < Lat. lingua — Eng. language, bilingual, Du. linguïstiek. Tongue = language, as in Du. taal/tong split.

notes.front: Estoy hasta las narices de sus excusas.
notes.back: I'm fed up to here with his excuses (lit. 'up to the nostrils').
notes.extra: Etymology: hasta < Arabic ḥattā — one of the few Arabic function words in Spanish. nariz < Lat. naris — Eng. nasal; Du. neus is the native cognate (PIE *nas-).

notes.front: Se me hace la boca agua solo de pensarlo.
notes.back: My mouth waters just thinking about it.
notes.extra:
Etymology: boca < Lat. bucca 'cheek' (replaced os) — Fr. bouche, Eng. buccal, and music's embouchure.
Hook: Same image as Du. het water loopt me in de mond.

notes.front: Más vale tarde que nunca.
notes.back: Better late than never — word-for-word the Dutch beter laat dan nooit.
notes.extra: Etymology: nunca < Lat. numquam 'not ever'.

notes.front: A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda.
notes.back: The early bird catches the worm (lit. 'God helps who rises early').
notes.extra: Etymology: madrugar < Vulgar Lat. *maturicare < maturus 'ripe, early' — Eng. mature, premature. One verb for 'get up early' — Dutch and English need a whole phrase.

notes.front: En boca cerrada no entran moscas.
notes.back: Silence keeps you out of trouble (lit. 'flies don't enter a closed mouth').
notes.extra: Etymology: mosca < Lat. musca — mosquito is just its Spanish diminutive, exported to Eng. and Du. (muskiet). Even musket traces back via a fly-named hawk.

notes.front: Con ese comentario diste en el clavo.
notes.back: With that comment you hit the nail on the head.
notes.extra:
Etymology: clavo < Lat. clavus 'nail' — Eng. clove (the nail-shaped spice); Du. kruidnagel uses the identical nail metaphor.
Hook: Same metaphor as Du. de spijker op de kop slaan.

notes.front: Estoy entre la espada y la pared.
notes.back: I'm between a rock and a hard place (lit. 'between the sword and the wall').
notes.extra: Etymology: espada < Lat. spatha < Gk — Eng. spade (the card suit ♠ comes from Italian spade 'swords'), spatula.

notes.front: Aprobar ese examen no es moco de pavo.
notes.back: Passing that exam is no small feat (lit. 'not turkey snot' — the wattle).
notes.extra: Etymology: pavo < Lat. pavo 'peacock' — Eng. peacock contains the same word (pea- < pavo). When turkeys arrived from America, Spanish recycled the peacock's name.

notes.front: Perdona, se me fue el santo al cielo.
notes.back: Sorry, I completely lost my train of thought (lit. 'my saint went off to heaven').
notes.extra: Hook: Said to come from preachers forgetting which saint they were discussing.

notes.front: Así matamos dos pájaros de un tiro.
notes.back: That way we kill two birds with one stone (lit. 'one shot') — Du. twee vliegen in één klap.
notes.extra: Etymology: pájaro < Lat. passer 'sparrow' — Eng. passerine. The sparrow became the generic bird.

notes.front: Últimamente estás siempre en las nubes.
notes.back: Lately you've always got your head in the clouds.
notes.extra: Etymology: nube < Lat. nubes — Eng./Du. nuance comes from Fr. nue 'cloud': a nuance is a cloud-like shading.

notes.front: La reforma de la cocina nos costó un riñón.
notes.back: The kitchen renovation cost us a fortune (lit. 'a kidney').
notes.extra: Etymology: riñón < Lat. ren — Eng. renal, adrenaline (ad + renes: the gland sits on the kidney).

notes.front: Después de tres intentos, tiré la toalla.
notes.back: After three attempts, I threw in the towel.
notes.extra:
Etymology: toalla < Germanic *thwahljō 'washcloth' — cognate with Du. dweil! A Germanic word that colonized Romance.
Hook: Boxing metaphor, identical in Du. (de handdoek in de ring gooien).

notes.front: Venga, ponte las pilas que llegamos tarde.
notes.back: Come on, get your act together, we're late (lit. 'put your batteries in').
notes.extra: Etymology: pila < Lat. pila 'pillar, heap' — Eng. pile; the battery sense comes from Volta's pile of metal discs (1800).

notes.front: El profesor hizo la vista gorda con los retrasos.
notes.back: The teacher turned a blind eye to the late arrivals (lit. 'made the fat view').
notes.extra: Hook: Du. een oogje dichtknijpen — same eye-based image, different mechanics.

notes.front: En su nuevo trabajo está como pez en el agua.
notes.back: In her new job she's in her element (lit. 'like a fish in water') — Du. als een vis in het water, identical.
notes.extra: Etymology: pez < Lat. piscis — Eng. Pisces; Du. vis and Eng. fish are the native cognates (PIE *peysk-). Three branches, one root.

notes.front: Anoche no pegué ojo por el ruido.
notes.back: Last night I didn't sleep a wink because of the noise (lit. 'didn't glue an eye').
notes.extra: Etymology: pegar < Lat. picare 'to smear with pitch' < pix — Eng. pitch. Gluing eyes shut with pitch = falling asleep.

notes.front: Creo que he metido la pata con tu hermana.
notes.back:
I think I put my foot in it with your sister.
• meter la pata = to blunder; pata = animal leg (cf. Fr. patte).
notes.extra: Etymology: meter < Lat. mittere 'to send, put' — Eng. mission, transmit, Du. missie.

notes.front: El examen teórico fue pan comido.
notes.back: The theory exam was a piece of cake (lit. 'eaten bread').
notes.extra: Etymology: pan < Lat. panis — hidden in Eng. company/companion and Du. kompaan: com-panis, someone you share bread with.

notes.front: Llueve a cántaros, mejor esperamos.
notes.back: It's bucketing down (lit. 'raining by the pitcherful'), better wait.
notes.extra: Etymology: cántaro < Gk kantharos (a wine vessel). Compare Eng. 'raining cats and dogs', Du. pijpenstelen — every language grabs a random object.

notes.front: Cuando me lo contaron, me quedé de piedra.
notes.back: When they told me, I was stunned (lit. 'I remained of stone').
notes.extra: Etymology: piedra < Lat. petra — Eng. petrify (the same metaphor!), petroleum ('rock-oil'), the name Peter, Du. petroleum.

notes.front: Su explicación no tiene ni pies ni cabeza.
notes.back: His explanation makes no sense at all (lit. 'has neither feet nor head') — Du. slaat kant noch wal.
notes.extra: Etymology: cabeza < Vulgar Lat. capitia < caput — Eng. captain, capital, Du. kapitein.

notes.front: No le busques tres pies al gato.
notes.back: Don't overcomplicate things (lit. 'don't look for three feet on the cat').
notes.extra: Etymology: gato < Late Lat. cattus — Eng. cat, Du. kat: Latin exported this word to all of Germanic.

notes.front: Hoy el jefe está de mala leche.
notes.back: The boss is in a foul mood today (lit. 'of bad milk' — from old beliefs about nursing).
notes.extra: Etymology: leche < Lat. lac, lactis — Eng. lactose, lettuce (named for its milky sap!), Du. lactose.

notes.front: Déjate de rodeos y ve al grano.
notes.back: Stop beating around the bush and get to the point (lit. 'go to the grain').
notes.extra: Etymology: grano < Lat. granum — Eng. grain, pomegranate ('seeded apple'), Du. graan; Du. koren is the native cognate of the same PIE root.

notes.front: Hay que tomar el toro por los cuernos.
notes.back: You have to take the bull by the horns — Du. de koe bij de horens vatten (the Dutch demoted it to a cow).
notes.extra: Etymology: cuerno < Lat. cornu — Eng. unicorn, corner; Du. hoorn is the native cognate (PIE *ḱer-).

notes.front: Después del maratón estaba hecho polvo.
notes.back: After the marathon I was wrecked (lit. 'turned to dust').
notes.extra: Etymology: polvo < Lat. pulvis — Eng. pulverize, powder, Du. poeder, and gunpowder = pólvora.

notes.front: No te duermas en los laureles.
notes.back: Don't rest on your laurels — Du. op je lauweren rusten, identical Greco-Roman heritage.
notes.extra: Etymology: laurel < Lat. laurus — Eng. laureate, baccalaureate ('laurel berry'), Du. laureaat.

notes.front: A caballo regalado no le mires el diente.
notes.back: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth — Du. een gegeven paard niet in de bek kijken, same proverb across Europe.
notes.extra: Etymology: caballo < Lat. caballus 'nag, workhorse', which ousted noble equus — Eng. cavalry, chivalry, Du. cavalerie.

notes.front: El que no llora, no mama.
notes.back: The squeaky wheel gets the grease (lit. 'who doesn't cry doesn't nurse').
notes.extra: Etymology: llorar < Lat. plorare — Eng. deplore, implore. Note Lat. pl- → Sp. ll-: plorare→llorar, pluere→llover, plenus→lleno.

notes.front: Cría cuervos y te sacarán los ojos.
notes.back: Raise crows and they'll peck your eyes out — on ingratitude.
notes.extra: Etymology: cuervo < Lat. corvus — Eng. corvid. criar < creare — Eng. create; raising kids = creating.

notes.front: No hay mal que por bien no venga.
notes.back:
Every cloud has a silver lining (lit. 'there's no bad that doesn't come for a good').
• Note the embedded subjunctive venga after the negated antecedent — grammar hiding inside a proverb.

notes.front: Al mal tiempo, buena cara.
notes.back: When the going gets tough, put on a brave face (lit. 'to bad weather, good face').
notes.extra: Etymology: cara < Gk kara 'head' — Eng. cheer descends from it via Old Fr. chiere 'face': 'good cheer' literally = 'good face', the exact same idiom.

notes.front: Vale, cada loco con su tema.
notes.back: Fine — to each his own obsession (lit. 'each madman with his theme').
notes.extra: Etymology: tema < Gk thema — Eng. theme, Du. thema. loco: origin disputed, possibly Arabic lawqā 'foolish'.

notes.front: Mi hermano y yo somos uña y carne.
notes.back: My brother and I are inseparable (lit. 'nail and flesh').
notes.extra: Etymology: uña < Lat. ungula — Eng. ungulate. carne < caro, carnis — Eng. carnival (Du. carnaval): carne vale, 'farewell, meat', before Lent; also carnivore, reincarnation.

notes.front: No eches más leña al fuego, por favor.
notes.back: Don't add fuel to the fire, please — Du. olie op het vuur gooien (Dutch upgraded wood to oil).
notes.extra: Etymology: fuego < Lat. focus 'hearth' — Eng./Du. focus: the hearth was the focal point of the Roman house; physics borrowed the word from there.

notes.front: En la final pusieron toda la carne en el asador.
notes.back: In the final they went all in (lit. 'put all the meat on the spit').
notes.extra: Etymology: asador < asar < Lat. assare 'to roast'.

notes.front: Es muy terco, nunca da su brazo a torcer.
notes.back: He's stubborn, he never gives in (lit. 'never lets his arm be twisted') — cf. Eng. 'arm-twisting'.
notes.extra: Etymology: brazo < Lat. bracchium — Eng. brace, bracelet, embrace, pretzel (Ger. Brezel < little arms!).

notes.front: Antes de decidir, voy a consultarlo con la almohada.
notes.back: Before deciding, I'll sleep on it (lit. 'consult it with the pillow') — Du. er een nachtje over slapen.
notes.extra: Etymology: almohada < Arabic al-mukhadda < khadd 'cheek'. The al- in Spanish words (almohada, algodón, alcalde) is the Arabic article fossilized in place.

notes.front: Sin embargo, no todo está perdido.
notes.back:
However, not everything is lost.
• sin embargo = the workhorse 'however'.
notes.extra: Etymology: embargo < Vulgar Lat. *imbarricare 'to bar' — Eng. embargo (a Spanish export!), barricade, bar, Du. barricade. Lit. 'without obstruction'.

notes.front: A pesar de todo, seguimos adelante.
notes.back:
In spite of everything, we carry on.
• a pesar de = despite.
notes.extra: Etymology: pesar < Lat. pensare 'to weigh' — despite something 'weighing on' you. Same root as pensar (thinking = weighing) and Du. pensioen.

notes.front: Por lo tanto, debemos actuar cuanto antes.
notes.back:
Therefore, we must act as soon as possible.
• por lo tanto = formal 'therefore'; cuanto antes = ASAP.
notes.extra: Etymology: actuar < Lat. actus — Eng. act, Du. actueel, acteren.

notes.front: En cuanto a tu propuesta, me parece razonable.
notes.back:
As for your proposal, it seems reasonable to me.
• en cuanto a = 'as regards' (≠ en cuanto + subj. 'as soon as').
notes.extra: Etymology: proponer < Lat. proponere 'to put forward' — Eng. propose, Du. propositie.

notes.front: No obstante, hay que tener cuidado.
notes.back: Nevertheless, one must be careful.
notes.extra: Etymology: no obstante < Lat. non obstante 'not standing in the way' — Eng. notwithstanding and legal Du. niettegenstaande are literal calques of the same Latin. Also Eng. obstacle, Du. obstakel.

notes.front: Además, el precio es bastante razonable.
notes.back: Besides, the price is quite reasonable.
notes.extra: Etymology: además < a + de + más; más < Lat. magis — Eng. master, magistrate, Du. magistraat (all 'greater' words).

notes.front: Es decir, tendremos que empezar de cero.
notes.back: That is to say, we'll have to start from scratch (lit. 'from zero').
notes.extra: Etymology: cero < Arabic ṣifr 'empty' — which also gave Eng. cipher AND Du. cijfer 'digit'. Dutch and Spanish took the same Arabic word for opposite ends of the number line.

notes.front: De hecho, ya lo habíamos previsto.
notes.back:
In fact, we had already foreseen it.
• de hecho = 'in fact' (< factum, like Eng. de facto).
notes.extra: Etymology: prever < Lat. praevidere — Eng. provide/providence come from the same 'seeing ahead'.

notes.front: Ahora bien, no todo son ventajas.
notes.back:
That said, it's not all advantages.
• ahora bien = discourse pivot before a caveat.
notes.extra: Etymology: ventaja < Old Fr. avantage < Lat. ab ante — Eng. advantage, Du. avanceren.

notes.front: Por consiguiente, la reunión queda cancelada.
notes.back:
Consequently, the meeting is cancelled.
• quedar + participle = resultant state (very common in formal notices).
notes.extra: Etymology: consiguiente < Lat. consequi 'to follow along' — Eng. consequence, Du. consequent.

notes.front: En resumen, fue un éxito rotundo.
notes.back: In short, it was a resounding success.
notes.extra: Etymology: éxito < Lat. exitus 'way out, outcome' — classic false friend of Eng. exit: the 'good outcome' sense won in Spanish. rotundo < rotundus 'round' — Eng. rotund, Du. rotonde.

notes.front: Dicho esto, respeto tu decisión.
notes.back:
That said, I respect your decision.
• dicho esto = absolute participle construction, straight from Latin ablative absolutes (his dictis).

notes.front: Por si acaso, llévate el paraguas.
notes.back: Just in case, take the umbrella.
notes.extra: Etymology: acaso < a + caso < Lat. casus 'a fall, chance' (< cadere) — Eng. case, casual, accident ('a falling upon'), Du. casus. paraguas = para ('stops') + aguas, built like parasol, parachute.

notes.front: A fin de cuentas, lo importante es la salud.
notes.back:
At the end of the day, health is what matters.
• a fin de cuentas = 'when the accounts are settled'.
notes.extra: Etymology: salud < Lat. salus — Eng. salute, salutary, Du. saluut. ¡Salud! = toast AND 'bless you'.

notes.front: Ella es muy sociable; en cambio, su hermano es tímido.
notes.back:
She's very sociable; her brother, by contrast, is shy.
• en cambio = 'on the other hand'.
notes.extra: Etymology: cambiar < Late Lat. cambiare (Gaulish loan) — Eng. change, exchange; you've seen CAMBIO at every Spanish exchange office.

notes.front: Desde luego, puedes contar conmigo.
notes.back:
Of course, you can count on me.
• contar con = to rely on.
notes.extra: Etymology: conmigo < Lat. cum + me + cum — Latin said mecum, Spanish forgot and re-added con, giving a double 'with'. contar < computare — Eng. count, compute, Du. computer.

notes.front: Sea como sea, mañana lo sabremos.
notes.back:
Be that as it may, we'll know tomorrow.
• Doubled subjunctive concessive (sea como sea, pase lo que pase, digan lo que digan) — a productive pattern worth stealing.

notes.front: Menos mal que trajiste el mapa.
notes.back:
Thank goodness you brought the map.
• menos mal que + indicative = 'luckily'.
notes.extra: Etymology: traer < Lat. trahere 'to pull' — Eng. tractor, attract, trace, Du. tractor.

notes.front: Lo hice por ti, no para ti.
notes.back:
I did it because of you, not for you (to have).
• por = cause/motive; para = recipient/goal. This minimal pair is the whole por/para distinction in one line.

notes.front: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho por mí.
notes.back:
Thanks for everything you've done for me.
• por after gracias (cause) and with 'on behalf of/for the sake of'.
notes.extra: Etymology: gracias < Lat. gratias (agere) — Eng. grace, gratitude, gratis, Du. gratis.

notes.front: Para ser extranjero, habla muy bien español.
notes.back:
For a foreigner, he speaks Spanish very well.
• para + infinitive = 'considering, by the standard of'.
notes.extra: Etymology: extranjero < Lat. extraneus 'outsider' — Eng. strange(r), extraneous. A stranger is literally 'someone from outside'.

notes.front: El informe tiene que estar listo para el viernes.
notes.back:
The report has to be ready by Friday.
• para + time = deadline; por + time = approximate/duration.
notes.extra: Etymology: viernes < Lat. dies Veneris 'Venus' day' — Du. vrijdag/Eng. Friday = Freya's day, the Germanic gods calqued onto the Roman ones.

notes.front: Cambié mi coche por uno más pequeño.
notes.back:
I traded my car for a smaller one.
• por = exchange ('in place of'); para here would mean the car is a gift for the smaller one — nonsense.

notes.front: El jefe está de vacaciones hasta el lunes.
notes.back:
The boss is on holiday until Monday.
• estar de + noun = temporary state/role (de viaje, de guardia, de moda).
notes.extra: Etymology: vacaciones < Lat. vacare 'to be empty, free' — Eng. vacation, vacant, Du. vakantie, vacature.

notes.front: La reunión es en la sala grande.
notes.back:
The meeting is (takes place) in the big room.
• Events use ser for location — the big exception to 'location = estar'.
notes.extra: Etymology: sala < Germanic *sal — Du. zaal is the native sibling; the word went Germanic → Romance → back into fancy Fr. salon.

notes.front: Mi hermana es muy lista, pero nunca está lista a tiempo.
notes.back:
My sister is very clever, but she's never ready on time.
• ser listo = clever (trait); estar listo = ready (state). The classic ser/estar minimal pair.

notes.front: Este libro es aburrido; por eso estoy aburrido.
notes.back:
This book is boring; that's why I'm bored.
• ser = property (boring), estar = experienced state (bored) — Spanish does with one verb pair what English does with -ing/-ed.
notes.extra: Etymology: aburrir < Lat. abhorrere 'to shrink back from' — Eng. abhor. Boredom began as revulsion.

notes.front: ¡Qué buena está la sopa hoy!
notes.back:
The soup is really good today!
• estar + adjective = how it strikes you right now; ser buena = general quality. Same logic as estás muy guapa ('you look great [today]').

notes.front: Está prohibido fumar en todo el edificio.
notes.back:
Smoking is forbidden in the whole building.
• estar + participle = resulting state (the passive with ser would describe the act of forbidding).
notes.extra: Etymology: prohibir < Lat. prohibere 'to hold back' — Eng. prohibit, Du. prohibitie.

notes.front: Se me olvidaron las llaves en casa.
notes.back:
I left my keys at home (lit. 'the keys forgot themselves on me').
• No-fault se: se + indirect object + verb agreeing with the thing (olvidaron ↔ llaves).
notes.extra: Hook: Spanish grammar deflects blame; compare blunt Du. ik ben mijn sleutels vergeten.

notes.front: Se me hace tarde, tengo que irme.
notes.back:
It's getting late on me, I have to go.
• hacerse tarde + dative of the affected person; irse = leave (vs ir = go somewhere), like Du. weggaan vs gaan.

notes.front: Aquí se come muy bien.
notes.back:
The food here is great (lit. 'here one eats very well').
• Impersonal se = Du. men, Fr. on, Eng. generic 'you/one'.

notes.front: Se venden pisos en este edificio.
notes.back:
Apartments for sale in this building.
• Passive se: verb agrees with pisos. The SE VENDE sign you see all over Spain.
notes.extra: Etymology: piso < pisar < Lat. pinsare 'to stamp, tread' — a floor is what you tread; then floor → flat, like Du. etagewoning.

notes.front: Se me rompió el móvil justo antes del viaje.
notes.back:
My phone broke on me right before the trip.
• No-fault se again.
notes.extra: Etymology: romper < Lat. rumpere — Eng. rupture, corrupt, bankrupt < It. banca rotta 'broken bench' — which Dutch borrowed as bankroet.

notes.front: No te metas donde no te llaman.
notes.back:
Mind your own business (lit. 'don't put yourself where they don't call you').
• meterse = to meddle; negative imperative = no + subjunctive (no te metas, never *no métete).

notes.front: Me da igual lo que piensen los demás.
notes.back:
I don't care what other people think.
• dar igual + subjunctive (piensen); lo que = 'what' (headless relative).
notes.extra: Etymology: demás < de + magis, the same magis as in además.

notes.front: Se trata de una decisión muy importante.
notes.back:
It's a matter of a very important decision.
• tratarse de = impersonal 'to be about' — never with a personal subject.
notes.extra: Etymology: tratar < Lat. tractare — Eng. treat, tract, Du. trakteren (which narrowed to 'treat someone to food').

notes.front: Nos llevamos muy bien desde el principio.
notes.back:
We've gotten along great from the start.
• llevarse bien/mal con = get along.
notes.extra: Etymology: llevar < Lat. levare 'to lift' — Eng. lever, elevate, relieve, levitate. Carrying grew out of lifting.

notes.front: Me arrepiento de no haber estudiado más.
notes.back:
I regret not having studied more.
• arrepentirse de + perfect infinitive (haber estudiado).
notes.extra: Etymology: < Lat. re-paenitere — Eng. repent, penitence, and pain's cousin poena lurks behind it.

notes.front: ¿Cómo se te ocurrió semejante idea?
notes.back:
How did such an idea occur to you?
• ocurrírsele a alguien = to pop into someone's head — the idea is the subject, you are the dative bystander.
notes.extra: Etymology: ocurrir < Lat. occurrere 'to run to meet' — Eng. occur, current; Du. concurrent ('competitor') = one who 'runs together' with you.

notes.front: Se ha vuelto muy desconfiado con los años.
notes.back:
He's become very distrustful over the years.
• volverse + adjective = involuntary change of character (one of the several 'to become' verbs: hacerse, ponerse, llegar a ser).
notes.extra: Etymology: volver < Lat. volvere — Eng. revolve, revolution, Du. revolutie.

notes.front: Me acabo de enterar de la noticia.
notes.back:
I've just found out the news.
• acabar de + infinitive = 'to have just'; enterarse de = find out.
notes.extra: Etymology: enterar < Lat. integrare 'to make whole' — being informed = being made complete. Eng. entire, integer, Du. integer ('honest': morally whole).

notes.front: Estoy deseando que llegue el verano.
notes.back:
I can't wait for summer to arrive.
• estar deseando que + subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: desear < Lat. desiderare, likely 'to be away from the stars' (de + sidus) — the same stars as in Eng. consider ('consult the stars') and desire. Astrology fossilized in verbs.

notes.front: Vale la pena intentarlo al menos una vez.
notes.back:
It's worth trying at least once.
• valer la pena = to be worth the trouble.
notes.extra: Etymology: pena < Lat. poena — Eng. pain, penalty, and Du. pijn: one of the oldest Latin loans in Dutch. Worth the pain, literally.

notes.front: Hay que aprovechar el buen tiempo mientras dure.
notes.back:
We should make the most of the good weather while it lasts.
• hay que = impersonal obligation; mientras + subjunctive (dure) for indefinite duration.
notes.extra: Etymology: aprovechar < Lat. profectus 'progress, profit' — Eng. profit, Du. profiteren (but without the Dutch word's negative sneer).

notes.front: No te preocupes, ya me encargo yo.
notes.back:
Don't worry, I'll take care of it.
• encargarse de = take charge of; final yo adds emphasis.
notes.extra: Etymology: cargar < Late Lat. carricare < carrus (a Gaulish word!) — Eng. charge, cargo, carry, car, Du. kar. One Celtic wagon spawned them all.

notes.front: Dale recuerdos a tu familia de mi parte.
notes.back:
Give my regards to your family.
• recuerdos = regards; de mi parte = on my behalf.
notes.extra: Etymology: recordar < Lat. recordari < cor 'heart' — remembering happened in the heart: Eng. record (originally 'learn by heart'), cordial, courage.

notes.front: ¿Te apetece salir a cenar esta noche?
notes.back:
Do you fancy going out for dinner tonight?
• apetecer works like gustar: the thing appeals to you.
notes.extra: Etymology: < Lat. appetere 'to reach for' — Eng. appetite, Du. appetijtelijk.

notes.front: No me atrevo a decírselo a la cara.
notes.back:
I don't dare say it to his face.
• atreverse a + infinitive; note the pile-up decír-se-lo (le→se before lo).
notes.extra: Etymology: < Lat. attribuere 'to claim for oneself' — Eng. attribute, tribute, Du. tribuut. Daring = arrogating.

notes.front: Merece la pena madrugar para ver el amanecer.
notes.back: It's worth getting up early to see the sunrise.
notes.extra: Etymology: merecer < Lat. merere 'to earn' — Eng. merit, Du. merites. amanecer < ad + mane 'toward morning' — Spanish has single verbs for dawn (amanecer) and dusk (anochecer).

notes.front: Echo mucho de menos a mis amigos de la universidad.
notes.back:
I really miss my university friends.
• echar de menos = to miss (Latin America prefers extrañar).
notes.extra: Etymology: echar < Lat. iactare 'to throw' — Eng. eject, jet, jettison, Du. jet. Lit. 'to throw at a lack'.

notes.front: Me cuesta concentrarme por las tardes.
notes.back:
I find it hard to concentrate in the afternoons.
• costar + infinitive = to find difficult (metaphorical cost); por las tardes = habitual time.

notes.front: Por fin conseguí que me devolvieran el dinero.
notes.back:
I finally got them to give me my money back.
• conseguir que + subjunctive (here imperfect: devolvieran).
notes.extra: Etymology: conseguir < Lat. consequi 'to catch up with' — Eng. consequence; achieving = catching what you chased.

notes.front: Llevo tres años viviendo en los Países Bajos.
notes.back:
I've been living in the Netherlands for three years.
• llevar + time + gerund = duration up to now — no perfect tense needed, unlike Eng./Du.
notes.extra: Etymology: país < Lat. pagus 'rural district' — Eng. pagan ('villager', the countryside converted last), peasant.

notes.front: Sigo sin entender por qué lo hizo.
notes.back:
I still don't understand why he did it.
• seguir sin + infinitive = 'to still not' — an elegant negative Dutch/English lack.

notes.front: Acabo de darme cuenta de mi error.
notes.back:
I've just realized my mistake.
• darse cuenta de = to realize; realizar = to carry out (false friend).
notes.extra: Hook: Du. zich realiseren matches the Spanish reflexive.

notes.front: Vuelve a intentarlo, no te rindas.
notes.back:
Try again, don't give up.
• volver a + infinitive = re-do; rendirse = surrender.
notes.extra: Etymology: rendir < Vulgar Lat. *rendere < reddere 'to give back' — Eng. render, surrender, rent, Du. rente ('interest': money given back).

notes.front: Deja de quejarte y haz algo.
notes.back:
Stop complaining and do something.
• dejar de + infinitive = stop doing.
notes.extra: Etymology: quejarse < Vulgar Lat. *quassiare < quassare 'to shatter' (freq. of quatere) — Eng. quash, concussion. Complaining = being shaken.

notes.front: Tengo muchas ganas de que llegue el fin de semana.
notes.back:
I'm really looking forward to the weekend.
• tener ganas de que + subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: gana is probably Gothic *ganō 'greed' — a Germanic survivor inside core Spanish, like Du. gunnen's family.

notes.front: Hazme caso, no vayas por esa carretera.
notes.back:
Listen to me, don't take that road.
• hacer caso a = to heed; irregular imperative haz; negative imperative no vayas.
notes.extra: Etymology: carretera < carro — that Gaulish carrus again: the road is literally 'the cart-way'.

notes.front: Cuenta conmigo para lo que necesites.
notes.back:
Count on me for whatever you need.
• lo que + subjunctive (necesites) = 'whatever' (unspecified).
notes.extra: Etymology: necesitar < Lat. necesse — Eng. necessary, Du. noodzakelijk is the native calque.

notes.front: Lo tengo en la punta de la lengua.
notes.back: It's on the tip of my tongue — Du. het ligt op het puntje van mijn tong, identical.
notes.extra: Etymology: punta < Lat. puncta < pungere 'to prick' — Eng. point, puncture, pungent, Du. punt.

notes.front: Cuando se lo dije, se puso rojo como un tomate.
notes.back:
When I told him, he turned red as a tomato.
• ponerse + adjective = sudden involuntary change (blushing, angry, nervous).
notes.extra: Etymology: tomate < Nahuatl tomatl — Spanish is the pipeline that pumped Nahuatl into Du./Eng.: tomaat, chocolade (< xocolatl), avocado (< ahuacatl).

notes.front: Cada vez hay más gente que trabaja desde casa.
notes.back:
More and more people are working from home.
• cada vez más = increasingly.
notes.extra: Etymology: gente < Lat. gens, gentis 'clan' — Eng. gentle, genteel, gentile: 'of good clan' → well-born → mild.

notes.front: Hoy en día casi nadie manda cartas.
notes.back:
Nowadays hardly anyone sends letters.
• hoy en día = nowadays; casi nadie = hardly anyone.
notes.extra: Etymology: mandar < Lat. mandare < manus + dare 'to give into the hand' — Eng. mandate, command, Du. mandaat. Sending began as entrusting.

notes.front: A lo mejor me paso por tu casa luego.
notes.back:
Maybe I'll drop by your place later.
• a lo mejor + indicative — unlike quizás/tal vez, which prefer subjunctive. pasarse por = drop by.

notes.front: De vez en cuando me gusta desconectar del todo.
notes.back:
Every now and then I like to switch off completely.
• de vez en cuando = occasionally; del todo = entirely.
notes.extra: Etymology: desconectar: Lat. nectere 'to bind' — Eng. connect, nexus, annex, Du. connectie.

notes.front: En cuanto pueda, te devuelvo la llamada.
notes.back:
As soon as I can, I'll call you back.
• en cuanto + subjunctive (pueda); present devuelvo for near future.
notes.extra: Etymology: devolver < de + volvere — 'to roll back'.

notes.front: Por mucho que insistas, no voy a cambiar de opinión.
notes.back:
No matter how much you insist, I'm not changing my mind.
• por mucho que + subjunctive = 'however much'.
notes.extra: Etymology: insistir < Lat. insistere 'to stand on' — Eng. insist; standing your ground, literally.

notes.front: Está claro que algo le pasa.
notes.back:
It's obvious something's up with him.
• está claro que + indicative (certainty); no está claro que would flip to subjunctive.
notes.extra: Etymology: claro < Lat. clarus — Eng. clear, declare, and Du. klaar, which drifted from 'clear' to 'ready/done'.

notes.front: Actualmente trabajo desde casa tres días por semana.
notes.back:
I currently work from home three days a week.
• actualmente = currently, NOT 'actually' (= en realidad).
notes.extra: Hook: Dutch gets it free: actueel means exactly this.

notes.front: En realidad, no me sorprende en absoluto.
notes.back:
Actually, it doesn't surprise me at all.
• en absoluto = 'not at all' (despite looking positive — cf. Fr. pas du tout).
notes.extra: Etymology: absoluto < Lat. absolutus 'set free, complete' — Eng. absolute, absolve, Du. absoluut.

notes.front: Estoy constipado desde el lunes.
notes.back:
I've had a cold since Monday.
• Beloved false friend: constipado = having a head cold, NOT constipated (estreñido).
notes.extra: Etymology: < Lat. constipare 'to cram together' — a stuffed nose vs a stuffed gut: same Latin, different organ per language.

notes.front: Mi hermana está embarazada de cinco meses.
notes.back:
My sister is five months pregnant.
• THE false friend: embarazada = pregnant, not embarrassed (avergonzado).
notes.extra: Etymology: < Port. baraço 'cord, noose' → hindered, encumbered → with child. Eng. embarrassed kept the 'hindered' sense.

notes.front: Este año la empresa ha tenido mucho éxito.
notes.back:
This year the company has been very successful.
• éxito = success (never 'exit' = salida).
notes.extra: Etymology: empresa < emprender < Lat. prehendere 'to grasp' — Eng. enterprise, apprehend, prison; an undertaking is something grasped.

notes.front: Es muy sensible; se lo toma todo a pecho.
notes.back:
He's very sensitive; he takes everything to heart.
• sensible = sensitive (Eng. 'sensible' = sensato); Du. sensibel sides with Spanish.
notes.extra: Etymology: tomar a pecho: pecho < Lat. pectus — Eng. pectoral, expectorate.

notes.front: No soporto que la gente llegue tarde.
notes.back:
I can't stand people arriving late.
• soportar = to bear/tolerate, NOT to support (= apoyar); + subjunctive here.
notes.extra: Etymology: < Lat. supportare 'to carry from below' — Du. supporter (the football fan) kept the English sense.

notes.front: ¡Qué casualidad encontrarte por aquí!
notes.back:
What a coincidence running into you here!
• casualidad = coincidence, NOT casualty (= víctima).
notes.extra: Etymology: Both from Lat. casus 'a fall of the dice' — chance in Spanish, disaster in English.

notes.front: Al parecer, van a volver a subir los impuestos.
notes.back:
Apparently, they're going to raise taxes again.
• al parecer = apparently; volver a subir = raise again.
notes.extra: Etymology: impuesto < Lat. imponere 'to place upon' — Eng. impose; old Du. impost was exactly this word for a tax.

notes.front: Hace falta mucha paciencia para este trabajo.
notes.back:
This job takes a lot of patience.
• hacer falta = to be needed (gustar-type).
notes.extra: Etymology: paciencia < Lat. pati 'to suffer' — Eng. patient (one who suffers), passion (the suffering of Christ), passive, Du. patiënt, passie.

notes.front: Me quedé sin batería en el peor momento posible.
notes.back:
My battery died at the worst possible moment.
• quedarse sin = to run out of / be left without.
notes.extra: Etymology: batería < Fr. battre < Lat. battuere — Eng. battery (originally a beating!), battle, combat, Du. batterij.

notes.front: Está lloviendo a mares; espera un rato.
notes.back:
It's pouring (lit. 'raining seas'); wait a bit.
• un rato = a while.
notes.extra: Etymology: mar < Lat. mare — Eng. marine, maritime; Du. meer and Eng. mere are the native cognates (PIE *móri), though Dutch demoted it to 'lake'.

notes.front: Cuanto antes empecemos, antes terminaremos.
notes.back:
The sooner we start, the sooner we'll finish.
• cuanto antes + subjunctive... future: the Spanish 'the X-er, the Y-er' pattern.
notes.extra: Etymology: empezar < en + pieza (Celtic *pettia 'piece' — Eng. piece): to begin = to cut into the first piece.

notes.front: Por poco pierdo el tren esta mañana.
notes.back:
I almost missed the train this morning.
• por poco + present tense for a past near-miss — a vivid 'historical present' quirk.
notes.extra: Etymology: perder < Lat. perdere — Eng. perdition; Du. borrowed Fr. perdu in the same family.

notes.front: Da igual quién tenga la culpa; hay que solucionarlo.
notes.back:
It doesn't matter whose fault it is; we have to fix it.
• quién tenga: subjunctive in the indirect question after da igual.
notes.extra: Etymology: culpa < Lat. culpa — Eng. culprit, culpable, and everyone's mea culpa.

notes.front: Más vale prevenir que curar.
notes.back: Prevention is better than cure — Du. voorkomen is beter dan genezen, the same proverb.
notes.extra: Etymology: curar < Lat. curare 'to care for' — Eng. cure, curator, manicure ('hand-care'), Du. kuur (a treatment course), curator.

notes.front: Ten en cuenta que mañana es festivo.
notes.back:
Bear in mind that tomorrow is a public holiday.
• tener en cuenta = take into account; irregular imperative ten.
notes.extra: Etymology: festivo < Lat. festum — Eng. feast, festival, and Du. feest: another early Latin loan Dutch made its own.

notes.front: Hemos quedado a las ocho en la puerta del cine.
notes.back:
We're meeting at eight at the cinema entrance.
• quedar (no reflexive) = to arrange to meet — one of the most useful social verbs.
notes.extra: Etymology: cine < Gk kinema 'movement' — Eng. kinetic; Du. went its own way with bioscoop, 'life-viewer'.

notes.front: Su cara me suena, pero no sé de qué.
notes.back:
Her face rings a bell, but I don't know from where.
• sonarle a alguien = to seem familiar (lit. 'to sound to someone').

notes.front: Lo siento, se me ha ido de la cabeza por completo.
notes.back:
Sorry, it's completely slipped my mind.
• írsele de la cabeza: the no-fault se applied to forgetting — the thought left on its own; you're innocent.

notes.front: No tengo ni idea de lo que estás hablando.
notes.back:
I have no idea what you're talking about.
• ni idea = emphatic 'no idea'.
notes.extra:
Etymology: ni < Lat. nec.
Hook: Du. geen flauw idee.

notes.front: ¿Me echas una mano con esto cuando puedas?
notes.back:
Can you give me a hand with this when you get a chance?
• echar una mano = lend a hand — Du. een handje helpen; cuando puedas = subjunctive for indefinite time.

notes.front: Dales las gracias de mi parte a tus padres.
notes.back:
Thank your parents for me.
• dar las gracias = to thank; clitic les doubles the explicit a tus padres — mandatory redundancy Spanish loves and Dutch would delete.

notes.front: Se hace de rogar, pero al final siempre viene.
notes.back:
He plays hard to get, but in the end he always comes.
• hacerse de rogar = to make people beg you.
notes.extra: Etymology: rogar < Lat. rogare 'to ask' — Eng. interrogate, arrogant ('claiming for oneself'), prerogative.

notes.front: Voy a apuntarme a un curso de fotografía.
notes.back:
I'm going to sign up for a photography course.
• apuntarse a = enrol; also 'count me in' (¡me apunto!).
notes.extra: Etymology: < punto < pungere: to sign up = to be marked with a point on the list.

notes.front: Quien mucho abarca, poco aprieta.
notes.back: Grasp all, lose all (lit. 'who embraces much, squeezes little') — the anti-multitasking proverb.
notes.extra: Etymology: abarcar < Lat. brachium 'arm' again: to embrace with the arms; apretar < Late Lat. appectorare 'to press to the chest' (pectus).

notes.front: Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres.
notes.back: Tell me who you walk with and I'll tell you who you are — Du. soort zoekt soort, but the Spanish is more elegant.
notes.extra: Etymology: andar probably < Lat. ambulare — Eng. amble, ambulance (originally a walking field hospital).

notes.front: El que mucho habla, mucho yerra.
notes.back: He who talks much, errs much.
notes.extra: Etymology: errar < Lat. errare 'to wander' — Eng. err, error, erratic, knight errant ('wandering'). To be wrong = to have wandered off.
